title: A Victory Song, Then Bitter Water
overview: Right after crossing the sea, Israel sings about the LORD defeating Egypt's army, and three days later they face their first water crisis in the desert.

parts.label: Praise for the rescue (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Moses and the people celebrate that the LORD, not they themselves, defeated Pharaoh's chariots and his best officers. Scholars widely regard this song as one of the oldest poems in the Bible, and Christians read it alongside Revelation 15, where the rescued sing 'the song of Moses and of the Lamb.'

parts.label: The sea and the enemy (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: God's 'right hand' and 'the blast of your nostrils' are poetic pictures of his strength, describing the wind that piled up the water and then let it crash back down. The song openly celebrates the drowning of the Egyptian soldiers, set against their boast that they would plunder and kill, and asks who among the gods could compare with the LORD, a way of saying nothing rivals him.

parts.label: Looking ahead to the land (vv. 13-18)
parts.note: The song turns to the future: neighboring peoples like the Philistines, Edom, Moab and Canaan will hear of this and freeze in fear while Israel passes through to the land God promised. The 'mountain' and 'sanctuary' may mean the land as a whole or the later temple in Jerusalem; scholars are unsure, and some think this part was shaped after Israel settled there.

parts.label: Miriam leads the women (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: Miriam, Aaron's sister and called a prophet, leads the women in dancing with tambourine-like hand drums, a common way women celebrated victories in that culture. Her short chorus repeats the song's opening line, possibly sung back and forth with the men.

parts.label: Bitter water at Marah (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: After three days without water they find only undrinkable water, so the place is named Marah, meaning 'bitter,' and the people turn on Moses. God shows Moses a piece of wood that makes the water drinkable, then uses the moment as a test: if they listen to him, he promises to be the one who heals them.

parts.label: Rest at Elim (v. 27)
parts.note: The journey reaches an oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees, a place of plenty right after the scare at Marah. Its exact location is uncertain, though older travelers linked it to a well-watered valley on the Sinai peninsula.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the sea crossing happened just as the song and story describe, with walls of water, or whether this is a poetic, heightened telling of a real escape whose details and location we cannot recover.
think: Why might relief after a crisis fade so quickly when the next problem shows up?
